content: A lisp, also referred to as a speech impediment or historically as sigmatism, is a condition that affects a person's ability to articulate certain speech sounds, particularly sibilants. Sibilants are sounds like the s or z sounds, which are often replaced with other sounds due to the nature of the lisp. There are several distinct types of lisps, each characterized by specific articulatory patterns. An interdental lisp occurs when the tip of the tongue protrudes between the upper and lower front teeth during speech. This results in the substitution of sibilant sounds with interdentals, leading to unclear articulation. A dentalized lisp is similar but slightly different in that the tip of the tongue makes contact with the back of the upper front teeth rather than protruding between them. This also affects the clarity of speech. A lateral lisp is characterized by the production of sounds like s and z with air escaping over the sides of the tongue. This type of lisp is often described as producing a slushy or wet sound, which is why it is sometimes referred to as a slushy ess or slushy lisp. The specific lateralized sounds associated with this type of lisp are represented in the Extended International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) for speech disorders. Lastly, a palatal lisp occurs when the speaker attempts to produce sibilant sounds with the tongue making contact with the palate, or the roof of the mouth. This articulation pattern also alters the intended sound, contributing to the speech impediment.
